title: The role of reverse cholesterol transport in animals and humans and relationship to atherosclerosis
authors: Rader DJ, Alexander ET, Weibel GL, Billheimer J, Rothblat GH
result: Review. Most peripheral cells cannot catabolise cholesterol and dispose of it by efflux to extracellular acceptors such as HDL. ABCA1 mediates efflux to lipid-poor apoA-I and ABCG1 efflux to mature HDL; LCAT esterifies HDL cholesterol; HDL cholesterol reaches the liver directly through SR-BI or after CETP-mediated transfer to apoB-containing lipoproteins and uptake by the LDL receptor; hepatic cholesterol is excreted into bile as cholesterol or after conversion to bile acids. Rodents lack CETP. A tracer study in healthy humans suggested that almost all HDL-derived labelled cholesterol excreted into bile was first transferred to apoB-containing lipoproteins. In animals, the rate of macrophage reverse cholesterol transport is more strongly associated with atherosclerosis than steady-state HDL cholesterol; methods to measure it in humans were still being developed and validated.
